teaser: Titian never sold this one. It stayed in his house until the day he died.
review_notes:
Date c. 1555 and Titian's age (birth year uncertain, c. 1488-90): approximate.
Lavinia's marriage in 1555 with a large dowry, and Titian's repeated letters about unpaid Spanish pensions: verify.
Painting still in Titian's house at his death in 1576, sold with the house by his son Pomponio to Cristoforo Barbarigo in 1581: verify.
X-radiograph: reused horizontal canvas with a double portrait of a man and woman, the man's jacket kept as Venus's wrap (National Gallery of Art technical study): verify.
Sold to Tsar Nicholas I in 1850; sold by the Soviet government to Andrew Mellon in 1931; given to the National Gallery of Art, opened 1941: verify.
Pose linked to the ancient “modest Venus” statue type: standard reading.

lesson.text: Around 1555 Titian was in his mid-sixties, give or take: even he was vague about his birth year. He was the most famous painter in Europe, with kings and an emperor for clients. He was also short of ready money. The Spanish court owed him years of unpaid pensions, and that same year he married off his daughter Lavinia with a handsome dowry. He wrote letter after letter asking to be paid.

In the middle of all this he painted a Venus that he sold to nobody. He kept her at home in Venice for the remaining two decades of his life. To understand why, start with how he made her, because the canvas has a secret that only X-rays revealed.

Underneath Venus lies another painting. X-ray images show that Titian began with the canvas turned sideways, for a double portrait of a man and a woman. He abandoned it, rotated the canvas a quarter turn, and painted the goddess on top.
He did not cover everything. One piece of the abandoned picture was too good to lose, and he worked it into the new one. You can still see it, along with the ancient idea that shaped her pose.

lesson.title: Old things reused
lesson.text: Three places where Titian recycles: a statue, a coat and a crown.

spots.title: The hand on the chest
spots.text: One hand to her breast, the other at her lap. The gesture comes from ancient marble statues known as the “modest Venus,” who covers herself as if surprised while bathing. Titian turns cold stone into warm skin.

spots.title: The red wrap
spots.text: Wine-red velvet, lined with fur and edged with gold and silver embroidery. This was the jacket of the man in the hidden portrait. Titian kept it and draped it around the goddess's hips.

spots.title: The wreath
spots.text: A winged child reaches up to set a ring of leaves and flowers on her head, one small hand resting on her shoulder. She is being crowned, and she does not even turn to look.

lesson.text: So what is she looking at? A second winged child, his back to you and a quiver strap across his shoulder, struggles to hold up a heavy mirror in a dark frame. You would expect it to show Venus admiring herself. Titian had a better idea.
Something in the mirror is looking back, and not at Venus. Find it.

spots.title: One eye
spots.text: The glass shows only a slice of her: a blurred cheek, a pearl earring, a shoulder, and a single sharp, dark eye. The angle is impossible for a woman looking at herself. That eye is aimed at you.

lesson.text: It is a quiet joke about looking. You came to stare at the goddess of beauty, and the mirror catches you doing it. Notice, too, how differently the two faces are painted: hers smooth and finished, the reflection a few loose, broken strokes. In his later years Titian painted more and more like that reflection.

The picture was still in his house when he died in 1576, during a plague epidemic. Five years later his son Pomponio sold the house and its contents, paintings included, to a Venetian nobleman named Barbarigo, whose family kept the Venus for nearly 270 years.

Why keep it? Probably for business. His workshop produced variant after variant of this Venus for collectors across Europe, and a master copy on the studio wall was the perfect model to work from. The painter who complained about unpaid kings had found a design that paid again and again.

In 1850 the Tsar of Russia bought it for the Hermitage in St. Petersburg. In 1931 the Soviet government, hungry for foreign cash, quietly sold it with other treasures to the American banker Andrew Mellon, who gave it to the new National Gallery of Art in Washington.

A recycled canvas, a borrowed statue pose, a design copied for decades: this painting shows a great artist at work as a practical man. The one thing he never repeated quite the same way is that single eye in the glass.

quiz.question: What did X-rays reveal under the painting?
options: An abandoned double portrait of a man and a woman
quiz.explanation: Titian turned the canvas a quarter turn and painted Venus over an unfinished portrait.

quiz.question: Where does the red fur-lined wrap come from?
options: It was the jacket of the man in the hidden portrait
It was added by a later restorer
It was copied from an ancient statue
quiz.explanation: Titian kept the man's jacket from the first picture and draped it around Venus.

quiz.question: What does the mirror show?
options: Part of her face, with one eye turned toward the viewer
quiz.explanation: The reflection holds a cheek, an earring and one sharp eye that looks out at us.

quiz.question: What happened to the painting during Titian's life?
options: He kept it in his house until he died
He sold it to the King of Spain
He gave it to his daughter as a dowry
quiz.explanation: It was still in his home at his death in 1576.

quiz.question: Who sold it to Andrew Mellon in 1931?
quiz.explanation: The Soviet state sold it from the Hermitage to raise foreign money.

facts.text: Titian painted this Venus on a fresh, unused canvas.
facts.explanation: He reused a canvas on which he had begun a double portrait.

facts.text: Her pose with one hand at her chest echoes an ancient statue type.
facts.explanation: It comes from the “modest Venus,” who covers herself as if surprised.

facts.text: Titian was rich in cash and well paid by the Spanish court in 1555.
facts.explanation: The Spanish court owed him years of pensions, and he kept writing to ask for payment.
